name: Lernaean Hydra
description: The Lernaean Hydra is a many-headed serpentine drakōn of Greek mythology, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, slain by Heracles as his second labor; its defining trait is the regrowth of two heads for each one severed.
full_description: The Lernaean Hydra (Greek Λερναῖα Ὕδρα) is a chthonic, multi-headed serpent-monster of Greek mythology that lurked in the springs of Lerna in the Argolid, near a reputed entrance to the Underworld. Hesiod's Theogony names her parents as Typhon and Echidna and her siblings as Cerberus, Orthrus, and the Chimera. Sources differ on the number of heads — six on early bronze fibulae (c. 700 BCE), nine in Alcaeus, fifty in Simonides, and indeterminate in Euripides and Virgil — but the regenerating-head motif, first attested in Euripides, became canonical: each severed head sprouted two more (or three, in Servius). Heracles, sent against the Hydra by King Eurystheus as his second labor, ultimately defeated her with the help of his nephew Iolaus, who cauterized each neck stump with a firebrand to prevent regrowth. The single immortal head was severed and buried under a great rock between Lerna and Elaius. Heracles dipped his arrows in the Hydra's venomous blood, providing him a deadly resource for later labors and ultimately the means of his own death through the Tunic of Nessus. The Hydra became proverbial in Greek and remains a stock image for problems that multiply when attacked.
origin: Mythological habitat is the marsh of Lerna, in the Argolid region of the Peloponnese, southern Greece, near a reputed entrance to the Underworld.

etymology.origin: Greek ὕδρα (húdra), 'water-snake', cognate with English 'otter' via the Indo-European root *wódr̥ ('water'). The name binds the creature to its watery lair at Lerna.
etymology.meaning: 'Water-snake of Lerna'; in classical usage 'Hydra' specifically denotes the Lernaean monster slain by Heracles.
etymology.first_use: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) is the earliest extant narrative reference; the figure appears on Boeotian bronze fibulae of the same era.

timeline.event: Boeotian bronze fibulae depict a hero attacking a six-headed water-serpent, c. 700 BCE
timeline.significance: Earliest visual attestation of the Hydra tradition

timeline.event: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) names the Hydra as offspring of Typhon and Echidna and sister of Cerberus and the Chimera
Alcaeus of Mytilene (c. 600 BCE) gives the Hydra nine heads
timeline.significance: Earliest specific head-count assignment in the canonical lineage

timeline.event: Euripides (5th c. BCE) attests the regenerating-heads motif
timeline.significance: First extant source for the iconic head-regrowth feature

timeline.event: Plato uses the Hydra as a logical metaphor in the Euthydemus (4th c. BCE)
timeline.significance: Early proverbial use of the Hydra for proliferating problems

timeline.event: Pseudo-Apollodorus's Bibliotheca (1st–2nd c. CE) gives the canonical Heracles-and-Iolaus account, including the immortal head buried under a rock
timeline.significance: Standard mythographic source for the second labor of Heracles

timeline.event: Pausanias's Description of Greece (2nd c. CE) locates the Hydra at the spring of Amymone
timeline.significance: Geographic anchoring of the myth in the Argolid

timeline.event: Servius (4th–5th c. CE) reports the variant of three heads regrowing per severance
timeline.significance: Late antique elaboration of the regeneration motif

timeline.event: Walter Burkert's Greek Religion published in English by Harvard University Press
timeline.significance: Standard modern reference framing the Hydra within Greek chthonic mythology

timeline.event: Daniel Ogden publishes Drakōn: Dragon Myth and Serpent Cult in the Greek and Roman Worlds (Oxford)
timeline.significance: Definitive modern study of Greek and Roman dragon-myth, including the Hydra

cultural_notes: In ancient Greek religion, the Hydra is firmly mythological — a child of Typhon and Echidna belonging to the chthonic order subdued by Olympian heroes — rather than a creature of folk sighting tradition.
